blocks.text: For she alone is heavy with young, while the other serpents, being oviparous, brood their offspring in the woods, enclosed in a shell. [col. 365] And Aelian, book 1, ch. 24: Τίκτει δὲ οὐκ ὠὰ, ἀλλὰ βρέφη, καὶ ἔστιν ἐνεργὰ ἤδη τὴν φύσιν αὐτῶν τὴν κακίστην· [Tiktei de ouk ōa, alla brephē, kai estin energa ēdē tēn physin autōn tēn kakistēn] But she bears not eggs but young, in which that most evil nature already shows itself. And Suidas: Ἔχις· εἶδος ὄφεως, ἀπὸ τοῦ κατέχειν, διότι μόνον τῶν ὄφεων οὐκ ὠοτοκεῖ, ἀλλὰ ζωοτοκεῖ· [Echis; eidos opheōs, apo tou katechein, dioti monon tōn opheōn ouk ōotokei, alla zōotokei] The viper, a kind of serpent, named from holding in (because it holds its young in the womb), because it alone of the serpents bears not eggs but a living animal. I reply that the viper, although it brings forth a living animal, nevertheless produces an egg inside, from which that animal comes forth. The Philosopher, On the Generation of Animals, book 1, ch. 10: Οἱ ἔχεις θύραζε μὲν ζωοτοκοῦσιν, ἐν αὐτοῖς δὲ ὠοτοκοῦσι πρῶτον, ὠοτοκοῦσι δὲ τέλειον ὠόν· οὕτως γὰρ γεννᾶται ἐκ τοῦ ὠοῦ τὸ ζῶον. [Hoi echeis thyraze men zōotokousin, en autois de ōotokousi prōton, ōotokousi de teleion ōon; houtōs gar gennatai ek tou ōou to zōon] Vipers indeed bring forth a living animal outwardly, but first they produce an egg within themselves, and that a perfect one: for thus the animal is generated from the egg. The same, History, book 3, ch. 3: Τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἄλλα γένη τῶν ὄφεων ὠοτοκεῖ· ἔχις δὲ ζωοτοκεῖ μόνον, ὠοτοκήσας ἐν αὑτῷ πρῶτον. [Ta men gar alla genē tōn opheōn ōotokei; echis de zōotokei monon, ōotokēsas en hautō prōton] The other kinds of serpents lay eggs; the viper alone generates a living animal, after first producing eggs within itself. And book 5, at the end: Τῶν δὲ ὄφεων ὁ μὲν ἔχεις ἔξω ζωοτοκεῖ, ἐν αὑτῷ πρῶτον ὠοτοκήσας· τὸ δὲ ὠὸν, ὥσπερ τῶν ἰχθύων, μονόχρουν ἐστὶ, καὶ μαλακόδερμον. [Tōn de opheōn ho men echeis exō zōotokei, en hautō prōton ōotokēsas; to de ōon, hōsper tōn ichthyōn, monochroun esti, kai malakodermon] Of the serpents the viper alone brings forth a living animal, having first produced eggs within itself; and its egg is of one color and soft, like those of fishes. Hence Pliny says of the viper: Of land animals she alone produces within herself eggs of one color and soft, like fishes. Some affirm this very thing from Theophrastus, History of Plants, book 7, ch. 14, where, after saying that τὴν ἀπαρίνην [tēn aparinēn], cleavers, produces a flower not visible but hidden within, he adds: ὥστε παρόμιον εἶναι τὸ συμβαῖνον, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν γαλεῶν, καὶ τῶν κρηνῶν· ἐκεῖνά τε γὰρ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ὠοτοκήσαντα ζωογονεῖ· [hōste paromion einai to symbainon, hōsper epi tōn galeōn, kai tōn krēnōn; ekeina te gar en heautois ōotokēsanta zōogonei] which Gaza rendered thus: So that it is like what happens in dogfish and vipers: for these, once they have produced eggs within themselves, presently give birth to living animals. That is, for the corrupt word κρηνῶν [krēnōn] he wanted to read ἐχιδνῶν [echidnōn]. I would prefer κυνῶν [kynōn] or ῥίνων [rhinōn]. If you follow the former, γαλεῶν [galeōn] and κυνῶν [kynōn] will be synonyms, and after τῶν γαλεῶν [tōn galeōn] Theophrastus will have added καὶ τῶν κυνῶν [kai tōn kynōn] by way of distinction, so that we might know that by the name τῶν γαλεῶν [tōn galeōn] are meant κύνας [kynas], sea-dogs, which are also called γαλεοὶ [galeoi]. But if for τῶν κρηνῶν [tōn krēnōn] you read τῶν ῥίνων [tōn rhinōn], angel sharks will be understood, which Oppian counts among the kinds of dogfish in these words, Halieutica, book 1, line 379:

[III, 135] — — — γαλεῶν δ' ἑτερότροπα φῦλα, Σκύμνοι, καὶ λείαι, καὶ ἀκανθίαι, ἐν δ' ἄρα τοῖσι 'Ρῖναι. — — — — — [galeōn d' heterotropa phyla, Skymnoi, kai leiai, kai akanthiai, en d' ara toisi Rhinai]

But there are diverse kinds of dogfish: scymni, and leae, and acanthiae; among these too are the angel sharks. Accordingly the Philosopher says that dogfish and angel sharks have this in common, that they receive their young within themselves and emit them, History, book 6, ch. 10. On this very point Oppian compares dogfish and angel sharks with one another, in line 742 of the same book. But whatever you read in Theophrastus, it is clear from Aristotle and Pliny that eggs are rightly attributed to the viper too, although she has them within herself and hidden in the womb: so that no one should find it strange that Isaiah spoke of the eggs of the viper.
